column1: What is the formula for contrast ratio according to CIE/WCAG colorimetry standards?
column2: Contrast Ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the relative luminance of the lighter color and L2 is the relative luminance of the darker color.

column1: What minimum contrast ratios are required for body text vs. fine detail under accessibility standards?
column2: ≥4.5:1 for body text, ≥7:1 for fine detail/small text.

column1: What are the four Gestalt grouping principles that drive automatic visual grouping?
column2: Proximity (spatial distance), Similarity (shared shape/color), Common Region (enclosure), and Continuity (aligned vectors).

column1: Name the three classic reading vector patterns used in layout design and when each applies.
column2: Gutenberg Diagram (primary optical area to terminal area, general reading), Z-Pattern (scanning open promotional layouts), F-Pattern (information-dense text parsing).

column1: What are three common typographic scale ratios used to derive hierarchical font sizes?
column2: Major Third (1.250), Perfect Fourth (1.333), and Golden Ratio (1.618).

column1: What determines 'visual weight' (optical mass) of an element in a composition?
column2: Area, luminance contrast, saturation, and geometric complexity.

column1: What is the core invariant of constraint-based design systems (grids, modular scales)?
column2: Restriction precedes variation—constraints (e.g., an 8px baseline grid or 12-column grid) establish a coordinate system that channels creativity rather than limiting it; rules must be established before they can be purposefully broken.

column1: In an 8-pixel baseline grid system, what is the purpose of deriving spacing values as multiples of 8 (16, 24, 32, 64)?
column2: It creates consistent vertical rhythm and perceptual harmony, so the eye perceives systematic proportional relationships rather than arbitrary spacing.

column1: Why does conscious visual processing create a 'serial bottleneck' that designers must account for in hierarchy design?
column2: Despite parallel preprocessing in the early visual cortex, conscious attention can only deeply process one semantic message at a time; without clear dominance hierarchy, the viewer faces a high-entropy signal environment causing cognitive friction.

column1: What seven dimensions can designers manipulate to encode visual dominance/hierarchy?
column2: Scale differential, spatial positioning, color saturation/value intensity, textural density, motion dynamics (time-based media), depth-of-field focus gradients, and typographic weight variation.

column1: What is the fundamental data-model incompatibility between vector and raster graphics?
column2: Vector graphics describe geometry via resolution-independent mathematical abstractions (Bézier curves, line segments) that scale infinitely without degradation; raster graphics encode fixed pixel grids bound to specific spatial resolution (PPI/DPI), degrading when scaled beyond their native resolution.

column1: Why does converting a design from RGB (screen) to CMYK (print) typically narrow the achievable color gamut?
column2: RGB uses additive color mixing (emitted light, brightens toward white) while CMYK uses subtractive color mixing (ink absorbs wavelengths, darkens toward black); these are opposing physical mechanisms, and many on-screen RGB colors fall outside the physical ink gamut, requiring perceptual remapping via rendering intent algorithms.
